concepts.def: Microscopic air sacs in the lungs providing a large, thin, moist surface for gas exchange.
Higher in small organisms, allowing exchange across body surface; falls with size, requiring specialised systems.
Blood and water flow in opposite directions across fish gills, maintaining a diffusion gradient along the entire length.
Pores on plant leaves (mostly underside) flanked by guard cells, regulating gas exchange and water loss.
Branching air tubes in insects delivering oxygen directly to tissues; close via spiracles.
Movement of air (or water) over the gas exchange surface to maintain steep diffusion gradients.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

mcqs.q: Counter-current flow in fish gills maintains:
options: A steady ATP supply
A concentration gradient along the gill
Constant temperature
High blood pH
Lungs
Gills
Trachea and spiracles
Skin

mcqs.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?
options: The enzyme has died because enzymes are alive.
Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
Its tertiary structure (3D shape) changes, particularly the active site, so it can no longer bind substrate effectively.
The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.

mcqs.q: Why is the secondary immune response to a pathogen faster and stronger than the primary?
options: Memory cells generated during the primary response can rapidly proliferate and produce large amounts of specific antibody on re-exposure.
Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
The pathogen becomes weaker after the primary exposure, so the body has an easier job.
The body produces a different, more powerful antibody during the secondary response.

mcqs.q: During an action potential, do Na+ and K+ move through the same channels?
options: Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
Na+ and K+ swap places through the same channel at the same time.
The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.
No — voltage-gated Na+ channels open first (depolarisation, Na+ in), then voltage-gated K+ channels open (repolarisation, K+ out).
